description: Oedipus saves Thebes by solving the riddle of the Sphinx. This victory of the spirit, however, opens the door to the most terrible tragedy.

hero.hook: A monster poses a riddle. Oedipus replies “Man”. He saves a city... and walks towards his own misfortune.

blocks.text: Before being the tragic hero who kills his father and marries his mother, **Oedipus** is first a savior. In front of **Thebes**, a city of Boeotia in central Greece, he confronts the **Sphinx**, a monster which devours anyone who fails his riddle.

He wins by the mind, not by the sword. But this victory places him on a throne where he will have to face what he does not know about himself. The myth opposes knowledge of man in general... and tragic ignorance of oneself.

The Sphinx is a divine punishment, often linked to **Hera**. Body of a lion, bust of a woman, wings of a bird, tail of a snake: a hybrid creature. Installed near the city, it cuts the roads. King **Laios** has disappeared, killed by an unknown person at a crossroads. The city is without a real leader.

blocks.caption: The Sphinx of Thebes, guardian of a deadly enigma.

blocks.text: Every passerby must respond. Failure means death. Even Regent  fails. The monster embodies the triumph of enigma over reason... until the arrival of a stranger named Oedipus. [[Creon]]

sections.title: A monster on the road to Thebes

blocks.text: Oedipus flees Corinth. An oracle predicted to him that he would kill his father and marry his mother. He believes he is avoiding fate. On the road to Thebes, the Sphinx asks his question: which being has four feet in the morning, two at noon, three in the evening?

blocks.caption: Oedipus facing the Sphinx, victory of intelligence.

blocks.text: The word **Sphinx** comes from the Greek *sphinx*, “to squeeze” or “to strangle”. It designates both the way the monster kills... and the way an enigma paralyzes the mind.

Oedipus responds: **“The Man”**. As a child, he crawls on all fours; as an adult, he walks on two legs; old, he leans on a cane. The Sphinx, defeated, throws itself from the rock. It's a brutal . Thebes is free. As promised, Oedipus receives the crown and the hand of the widowed queen, **Jocasta**. [[turnaround]]

sections.title: “Which being has four, two, then three feet? »

blocks.text: Oedipus reigns. The city prospers. But a plague strikes later. **Apollo** reveals: the scourge will end when the murderer of Laius is found. Oedipus launches an investigation with the same energy as before facing the Sphinx.

The irony is cruel. Whoever defined “Man” does not know who he is. He has won a public , a duel of arguments, but remains blind to his identity. In **Sophocles**, in *Oedipus King*, it is the heart of the tragedy. [[dialectics]]

sections.title: Knowing everything… except who you are

blocks.text: The truth comes out: Oedipus killed Laius, his father, and married Jocasta, his mother. Jocasta commits suicide. Oedipus gouges out his eyes. Having become blind, he finally “sees”. He wanders, supported by his daughter Antigone, himself becoming the three-legged old man of the enigma.
**Freud** named the [[Oedipus complex]] after this myth: not to make Oedipus a monster, but to talk about unconscious desires that civilization learns to repress.
The story becomes a pillar of Western culture: brilliant intelligence, inevitable destiny, and the terrible price of the truth about oneself.
Oedipus liberates Thebes by answering “Man” to the riddle of the Sphinx. This brilliance does not prevent him from realizing, without knowing it, the prophecy: the myth of self-deception.
